nameStory: Coelastrum cruciatum gets its name from its distinctive cross-shaped cell arrangements - 'cruciatum' means 'cross-like' in Latin. The genus name Coelastrum comes from Greek words meaning 'hollow star,' referring to the way these microscopic algae form star-like hollow colonies that look like tiny green snowflakes floating in water.
description: **[UNCERTAINTY FLAG: Limited reference material available]** Coelastrum cruciatum is a microscopic freshwater green algae that forms beautiful geometric colonies visible only under magnification. Each colony consists of 4-32 individual cells arranged in precise cross-shaped or star-like patterns, creating what looks like living green jewelry suspended in pond water. These colonies are typically only 20-100 micrometers across - far too small to see with the naked eye. You'll need a microscope to appreciate the intricate beauty of these aquatic microorganisms.

idTips.label: Cross-shaped cell arrangement
idTips.description: Under a microscope, cells are arranged in distinctive crosses or plus-sign patterns within each spherical colony, unlike the random arrangements of many other algae

idTips.label: Hollow colony structure
idTips.description: Colonies appear as hollow spheres with cells positioned only on the outer surface, creating a delicate lattice-work appearance when viewed from different angles

idTips.label: Bright green coloration
idTips.description: Cells display a vibrant emerald green color due to chlorophyll, appearing jewel-like when illuminated under microscope light

idTips.label: Small colony size
idTips.description: Colonies typically contain 8-16 cells arranged in their characteristic cross pattern, smaller than many related species

habitat: **[UNCERTAINTY FLAG: Limited observation data - only 2 recorded in New England]** Found in freshwater ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, particularly in nutrient-rich waters. Look for them in the plankton of small woodland ponds, farm ponds, and quiet backwaters where organic matter provides nutrients.

seasonality.spring: **[UNCERTAINTY FLAG]** Populations begin growing as water temperatures warm, often appearing in early spring pond samples when examined under magnification.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when conditions are optimal for photosynthesis and reproduction in pond ecosystems.
seasonality.fall: Populations may persist into fall but begin declining as temperatures drop and daylight hours decrease.
seasonality.winter: Generally not active during winter months, though some may survive in dormant stages until spring warming.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, a single drop of pond water can contain hundreds of these geometric living crystals, each one a perfectly organized microscopic city of cells working together - like finding an entire civilization hiding in what looks like empty water!
confusionNotes: **[UNCERTAINTY FLAG]** Most easily confused with other Coelastrum species, but the distinctive cross-shaped arrangement of cells sets it apart from the more star-like patterns of relatives like Coelastrum astroideum or the different geometric arrangements in Coelastrum pulchrum.
contextualKnowledge: Like many microscopic algae, Coelastrum species were largely unknown to science until the development of powerful microscopes in the 19th century, revealing an entire hidden world of geometric beauty in ordinary pond water that had been invisible to human eyes for millennia.
compareHints: **[UNCERTAINTY FLAG]** Coelastrum cruciatum differs from its relatives by its distinctive cross-shaped cell arrangements - C. astroideum forms more star-like patterns, while C. pulchrum creates more complex geometric designs. The 'cruciatum' species typically has fewer cells per colony and more pronounced cross-shaped symmetry than other members of the genus.
